cemc-cayley-1998-04.title: List factor pairs
cemc-cayley-1998-04.body:
The factor pairs of $100$ are $1\times100$, $2\times50$, $4\times25$, $5\times20$, $10\times10$, with sums $101, 52, 29, 25, 20$. The largest is $101$.

**Answer: (B) 101**

cemc-cayley-1998-05.title: Find the width
cemc-cayley-1998-05.body:
Triangle $BDC$ has area $\frac12\cdot DC\cdot BC=6\cdot BC=30$, so $BC=5$. The perimeter is $2(12+5)=34$.

**Answer: (A) 34**

cemc-cayley-1998-05.title: Half the rectangle
cemc-cayley-1998-05.body:
The diagonal splits the rectangle into two equal triangles, so the rectangle's area is $60$. Then $BC=60\div12=5$ and the perimeter is $12+5+12+5=34$.

**Answer: (A) 34**

cemc-cayley-1998-07.title: Co-interior angles
cemc-cayley-1998-07.body:
Let the two lines meet $AB$ at $M$ and $CD$ at $N$ (left line) and $P$ (right line). Since $AB\parallel CD$, the co-interior angles $\angle BMN$ and $\angle MND$ add to $180^\circ$: $2x+70=180$, so $x=55$. In triangle $MNP$: $y=180-70-55=55$.

**Answer: (D) 55**

cemc-cayley-1998-07.title: Alternate angles
cemc-cayley-1998-07.body:
From $2x+70=180$ we get $x=55$. The angle $y^\circ$ at $P$ and the angle $x^\circ$ between $MP$ and $MB$ are alternate angles between the parallel lines, so $y=x=55$.

**Answer: (D) 55**

cemc-cayley-1998-08.title: Base and height
cemc-cayley-1998-08.body:
The side from $(1,1)$ to $(7,1)$ is horizontal with length $6$. The third vertex $(5,3)$ is $2$ units above that line. Area $=\frac12\cdot6\cdot2=6$.

**Answer: (C) 6**

cemc-cayley-1998-12.title: Central angles
cemc-cayley-1998-12.body:
Join $C$ to all five vertices. In a regular pentagon these five angles at $C$ are equal: $360^\circ\div5=72^\circ$ each. The angle $x^\circ$ (from the top vertex to the lower-right vertex) spans two of them: $x=144$.

**Answer: (A) 144**

cemc-cayley-1998-13.title: Find the edge
cemc-cayley-1998-13.body:
A cube has $6$ equal square faces, so each face has area $54\div6=9$ and the edge is $3$. Volume $=3^3=27$.

**Answer: (D) 27**

cemc-cayley-1998-14.title: Count values of $x$
cemc-cayley-1998-14.body:
For each positive integer $x$, $y=100-3x$ is an integer, and it is positive exactly when $3x<100$, i.e. $x\le33$. So there are $33$ solutions.

**Answer: (A) 33**

cemc-cayley-1998-16.title: Equal small triangles
cemc-cayley-1998-16.body:
Triangle $ABC$ has area $\frac12\cdot9\cdot5=\frac{45}{2}$. The five triangles $ABW, WBX, XBY, YBZ, ZBC$ have equal bases on $AC$ and the same height from $B$, so each has area $\frac{45}{2}\div5=\frac92$. The same holds for the five triangles with vertex $D$. The shaded region is made of four of these small triangles: $4\cdot\frac92=18$.

**Answer: (C) 18**

cemc-cayley-1998-16.title: Fraction of the rectangle
cemc-cayley-1998-16.body:
The ten small triangles (five on each side of $AC$) all have equal area and fill the rectangle of area $45$. Four of them are shaded, so the area is $\frac4{10}\cdot45=18$.

**Answer: (C) 18**

cemc-cayley-1998-17.title: Exponents divisible by 3
cemc-cayley-1998-17.body:
A number is a perfect cube exactly when every exponent in its prime factorization is a multiple of 3. So $p+4$ is a multiple of 3 (smallest positive $p$ is $2$) and $q$ is a multiple of 3 (smallest $q=3$). Smallest $p+q=5$.

**Answer: (A) 5**

cemc-cayley-1998-19.title: Range of totals
cemc-cayley-1998-19.body:
Boys: $3$ to $9$. Girls: $15$ to $22$. The class size can be any whole number from $3+15=18$ to $9+22=31$. It must also be more than $25$: sizes $26,27,28,29,30,31$, which is $6$ sizes.

**Answer: (B) 6**

cemc-cayley-1998-20.title: Coordinates
cemc-cayley-1998-20.body:
Let $D=(0,0)$, $A=(0,8)$, and $BC$ be the line $x=8$. The centre is on the perpendicular bisector of $AD$, the line $y=4$, and is at distance $r$ from $x=8$, so it is $(8-r,4)$. Its distance to $D$ is $r$: $(8-r)^2+16=r^2$, so $80-16r=0$ and $r=5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

cemc-cayley-1998-20.title: Right triangle
cemc-cayley-1998-20.body:
Let $O$ be the centre and $M$ the midpoint of $AD$; $OM\perp AD$. The tangent point on $BC$ is level with $M$, so $OM=8-r$ and $MD=4$. Pythagoras in $\triangle OMD$: $(8-r)^2+4^2=r^2$, giving $r=5$ (a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle).

**Answer: (B) 5**

cemc-cayley-1998-21.title: Find $a$ and $c$
cemc-cayley-1998-21.body:
$x=1$: $a-2+c=-5$, so $a+c=-3$. $x=4$: $64a-8+c=52$, so $64a+c=60$. Subtracting, $63a=63$, so $a=1$ and $c=-4$. The expression is $x^3-2x-4$, and $x=2$ gives $8-4-4=0$.

**Answer: (A) 2**

cemc-cayley-1998-21.title: Factor
cemc-cayley-1998-21.body:
With $a=1$, $c=-4$: $x^3-2x-4=(x-2)(x^2+2x+2)$, and $x^2+2x+2=(x+1)^2+1>0$, so $x=2$ is the only real zero. Checking the other choices, e.g. $x=3$ gives $17\ne0$.

**Answer: (A) 2**

cemc-cayley-1998-22.title: Where the wheel stops
cemc-cayley-1998-22.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of the semicircle. When the wheel touches the semicircle, its centre $W$ is at height $8$ and $OW=25-8=17$ (the circles are tangent internally). The horizontal distance from $O$ to $W$ is $\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=15$, and the wheel touches the diameter directly below $W$.

So the wheel can touch only points within $15$ of $O$. On each side $25-15=10$ is untouched, a total of $20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

cemc-cayley-1998-23.title: Eliminate
cemc-cayley-1998-23.body:
From $5a+3b+5c=4a+5b+4c$ we get $a+c=2b$. Then $N=5(a+c)+3b=13b$. The only multiple of 13 between 131 and 150 is $143$, so $b=11$ and $a+b+c=3b=33$. (For example $a=1$, $c=21$ works: all four numbers are different.)

**Answer: (D) 33**

cemc-cayley-1998-23.title: Add the equations
cemc-cayley-1998-23.body:
Adding gives $2N=9(a+c)+8b$, and from $a+c=2b$ this is $26b$, so again $N=13b$; $N=143$, $b=11$, $a+b+c=33$.

**Answer: (D) 33**
